analogy.p: Imagine a rope held between two teams. On the side where both teams pull the same way the rope is pulled hard, and on the side where they pull against each other the pull is weak; the rope slides towards the weak side. In the motor effect the wire's field and the magnet's field add on one side and cancel on the other, and the wire is pushed to the weaker side. It breaks down because the wire is not pulled by ropes: no contact is involved and the force is at right angles to the fields.
analogy.t: Tug of war between two fields

bullets: **Definition (board wording):** when a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on one another. This is called the **motor effect**.
Needs **three things**: a conductor (usually a wire), a **current** in that conductor, and an external **magnetic field** (from a permanent magnet or an electromagnet).
If any one of these is missing (no current, no field) there is **no force**.
The force is a **non-contact force** acting on the wire, even though nothing touches it: the magnetic field acts at a distance.
The effect is the **reverse** of the generator effect (a conductor moving in a field makes a potential difference). Motor effect: electrical energy in, movement out.
This topic sits in **4.7 Magnetism and electromagnetism** and needs the earlier ideas of magnetic field lines (N to S outside the magnet) and the field around a current-carrying wire.
core.p: The **motor effect** is the name for the force experienced by a **current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field**. When a wire carrying a current sits in a magnetic field, the magnet that produces the field and the wire exert a force on **one another**. This is the key idea behind every electric motor, and it explains how a loudspeaker makes sound. It only works if there is both a current and a magnetic field, and the wire must not be lying along the field lines.

bullets: Field direction is defined as the direction of the force on a **north pole** placed at that point, so it points **away from N and towards S**.
**Closer field lines = stronger field.** Field strength is measured as **magnetic flux density** B in **tesla (T)**.
A **uniform field** has parallel, equally spaced lines (as between flat opposite poles); the force on the wire is then the same wherever it sits in the gap.
Magnetic field lines never cross and form closed loops (inside the magnet they continue from S to N).

Only the **magnetic materials** iron, steel, cobalt and nickel (and alloys with them) are attracted to magnets, but **any** wire carrying a current in a field feels the motor effect, whatever metal it is made from.
Link: this reuses the Year 10 work on permanent and induced magnets.
core.h: Magnetic fields you need to know first
core.p: A **magnetic field** is the region around a magnet (or a current-carrying wire) where a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force. Field lines show its shape and direction. Outside a bar magnet, field lines run from the **north pole to the south pole**, and the lines are closest together where the field is **strongest** (at the poles). Between two opposite poles facing each other (like the N and S poles of a horseshoe magnet) the field is almost **uniform**: straight, parallel, equally spaced lines. This uniform region is where we usually place the wire.

bullets: Field lines around a straight wire are **concentric circles**, getting **further apart** as distance from the wire increases (field weaker).
**Reverse the current** and the field lines around the wire reverse direction.
**Increasing the current** makes the wire's field **stronger**.
Right-hand grip rule: thumb = conventional current, curled fingers = direction of the wire's field.

A current going **into the page** is drawn with a **cross** (the tail feathers of an arrow going away); a current coming **out of the page** is drawn with a **dot** (the tip of an arrow coming at you).
Into the page gives **clockwise** field circles; out of the page gives **anticlockwise** circles.
Link: this is the same field idea that explains solenoids and electromagnets.
core.h: The magnetic field around a current-carrying wire
core.p: A current in a wire creates its **own magnetic field** in the form of **concentric circles** around the wire, in planes at right angles to it. The field is strongest close to the wire and weakens with distance (the circles get further apart). The direction of the circles depends on the direction of the current and is found with the **right-hand grip rule**: point the right thumb along the conventional current direction and the curled fingers show the direction of the field lines. It is the interaction of this circular field with the external field that produces the motor effect.

bullets: Take a uniform field pointing left to right and a current going into the page. The wire's clockwise field points **right above** the wire (adds to the uniform field) and **left below** it (cancels part of it).
So the field is **stronger above** and **weaker below** the wire, and the wire is pushed **downwards** (see Figure 3).
The field lines are **crowded** on one side and **sparse** on the other, which is the diagram clue for the direction of force.
The resultant force on the wire is at **right angles to both** the wire (current) and the external field.
This explanation is **qualitative**: it tells you where the force points, while F = BIl (next spec point) tells you how big it is.
Examiners accept: 'the magnetic field of the wire interacts with the field of the magnet, producing a force on the wire'.
Newton's third law applies: the wire also pushes back on the magnet with an equal and opposite force (see below).
core.h: Why the force arises: the catapult field
core.p: The force happens because two magnetic fields **overlap**: the uniform field of the magnet and the circular field of the wire. On one side of the wire the two fields point in the **same direction** and **add together** (a stronger field). On the other side they point in **opposite directions** and partly **cancel** (a weaker field). The result is a distorted field pattern sometimes called a **catapult field**, because it behaves like a stretched elastic band: the wire is pushed from the region of strong field **towards the region of weak field**.

bullets: **Left hand** for the motor effect (the right hand is for the right-hand grip rule and does not apply here).
**Thumb = Force (Motion), First finger = Field, Second finger = Current**: remember the initials F, B, I or 'thuMb, First, seCond'.
The three directions are **mutually at right angles** (90 degrees to each other); see Figure 2.
Use **conventional current**: from the positive terminal of the cell round to the negative, never the electron direction.
The field direction is from the **north pole to the south pole** of the magnet.
This is **Higher tier only** content in the AQA specification; Foundation students just describe that the force is at right angles.
The rule works because the force direction follows the direction of the cross product of current and field, but you only need to use the hand.
core.p: **Fleming's left-hand rule** is a quick way to find the direction of the force without drawing field lines. Hold the **thumb, first finger and second finger of your LEFT hand at right angles to each other**. The **thuMb** points in the direction of the **Force** (the **M**otion of the wire), the **First finger** points in the direction of the magnetic **Field** (north to south), and the **seCond finger** points in the direction of the **Current** (conventional current, positive to negative). The rule represents the **relative orientations** of the force, the current and the field.

bullets: Step 1: find field direction (N to S). Step 2: find conventional current direction (+ to -).
Step 3: first finger along the field, second finger along the current, both at right angles.
Step 4: the thumb points in the direction of the force on the conductor.
Example: field to the **right**, current **into the page**: the force is **down** the page (Figure 1). Check with the catapult idea: field stronger above, so push down. They agree.
If a question gives a diagram with dots and crosses, remember cross = into page, dot = out of page.
If you cannot get your hand to fit, you may have used the wrong hand or the wrong direction of current; recheck both.
In a 6-mark question you can state the direction and then **explain** it with fields interacting.
core.h: Using the rule step by step
core.p: Always use the same routine so you do not lose marks. First work out the direction of the **field** (N to S) and the direction of the **conventional current**. Then orient your left hand so that your **first finger points along the field** and your **second finger points along the current**; if your hand is held correctly the **thumb shows the force**. Practise with a real hand and a pencil, because the page is two-dimensional and your hand makes it three-dimensional.

bullets: Reverse the **current only** -> force reverses (Figure 4, top right).
Reverse the **field only** -> force reverses (Figure 4, bottom left).
Reverse **both** -> force is **unchanged** (two reversals cancel).
How to reverse the current: swap the connections on the battery or power supply. How to reverse the field: swap the magnet's poles (turn the magnet through 180 degrees).
With an **alternating current**, the current keeps reversing so the force on the wire keeps reversing: the wire vibrates (this is how a loudspeaker cone vibrates).
The size of the force stays the same when you reverse the direction; only the direction changes.
Mark scheme phrase: 'the force reverses if the current or the field direction is reversed'.
core.p: The direction of the force is **reversed** if **either** the **current** or the **magnetic field** is reversed, but if **both** are reversed the force stays the **same** direction. This is a very common exam question, and the cause is found directly from Fleming's rule: the thumb flips when only one of the other two fingers flips. Reversing the current means swapping the cell connections (or using alternating current); reversing the field means turning the magnet round so the poles swap sides.

bullets: Wire **perpendicular** to field: **maximum force**.
Wire **parallel** to field: **zero force**, even with a large current.
Between 0 and 90 degrees: a force somewhere between zero and maximum (not needed numerically at GCSE).
Only the length of wire **inside the field** counts; the parts of wire outside the magnet gap feel no force.
If there is **no current** (switch open), the wire is not a magnet, so there is no force.
This is why motor coils are arranged so that the sides cutting the field are at right angles to it.
Exam hint: 'the wire is parallel to the field so no force' is a classic 1-mark explanation.
core.h: When is there a force? Angle of the wire to the field
core.p: The size of the force depends on the angle between the wire and the field. The force is **largest** when the wire is at **right angles (perpendicular)** to the field lines, and the spec equation F = BIl applies in this case. If the wire lies **parallel** to the field lines there is **no force** at all, because the wire's circular field is then never aligned to add or cancel with the uniform field. At angles in between, only the part of the field at right angles to the wire contributes, so the force is smaller.

bullets: Stronger magnet (higher B, in tesla) -> larger force.
Larger current I (in amps) -> larger force.
Longer length of wire l in the field (in metres) -> larger force; many turns in a coil effectively multiply the length.
Force is directly proportional to current: a graph of F against I is a **straight line through the origin**.
In a motor, increasing the number of turns, the current or the magnet strength makes the motor turn faster or with more turning effect.
Force is measured in **newtons (N)**.
To investigate: use a current-carrying wire on a balance and a magnet underneath; see the practical section.
core.h: What affects the size of the force
core.p: The force on the wire increases when the **magnetic flux density** increases, when the **current** increases, and when the **length of wire in the field** increases. These three come straight from the equation **F = B I l** (force = magnetic flux density x current x length), which is covered in detail in the next spec point. For a given wire at right angles to the field, doubling the current doubles the force, so force and current are **directly proportional**.

bullets: Force on wire by magnet = force on magnet by wire, but opposite in direction.
The two forces act on **different objects**, so they do not cancel each other out.
Demonstration: place a magnet on a top-pan balance with a wire held in a stand across the poles; switching on the current changes the reading on the balance.

If the force on the wire is down, the wire pushes the magnet **up**, so the balance reading goes **down**; the change in reading gives the size of the force (mass change x gravitational field strength).
Link to Forces (4.5): resultant force, Newton's laws and free-body diagrams.
Describe in exam answers: 'the magnet exerts a force on the wire and the wire exerts an equal and opposite force on the magnet'.
core.h: Newton's third law and the motor effect
core.p: The spec says the magnet and the conductor exert a force **on one another**. This is **Newton's third law**: when two objects interact, the forces they exert on each other are **equal in size and opposite in direction**. So when the field pushes the wire down, the wire pushes the magnet up with an equal force. This is not usually noticeable because the magnet is heavy or fixed, but it can be measured with a top-pan balance.

bullets: Method: connect the wire in a circuit with a switch and low-voltage supply, place it between opposite poles, close the switch and observe the movement.
Observation: the wire **moves at right angles** to both the field and itself, never along the field lines.
Reverse the supply connections: the wire moves the **other way**. Swap the magnet: the wire moves the other way.
Use a stronger magnet or a larger current: the wire moves faster or further (greater force).
**Safety:** keep the current on for a short time only (heating), keep magnets away from electronics and cards.
Control variables when comparing: same wire, same position in the field, same distance between poles.
These ideas feed into the practical-skills exam questions on describing and improving a method.
core.p: Typical classroom demonstrations show the motor effect and prove the rules above. A common one is a **'jumping wire'**: a short length of copper wire (or a metal rod resting on two rails) is placed across the gap of a **U-shaped (horseshoe) magnet** and connected to a low-voltage supply. When the switch is closed the wire jumps or rolls, and you can reverse the current or the magnet to show the reversal. Always use a low-voltage power supply and do not leave the current on, because the wire and the supply can get hot.

bullets: **DC motor:** the commutator reverses the current every half turn so the coil keeps turning the same way (spec 4.7.2, next topics).
**Loudspeaker:** AC in the coil -> force alternates -> cone vibrates -> pressure waves (sound) at the same frequency as the AC.
Link to Energy (4.1): electrical energy is transferred to kinetic energy, plus wasted heating.
Link to Electricity (4.2): current direction and circuits.
Link to Forces (4.5): the force on the wire is a vector with a direction.

Contrast: the **generator effect** converts movement to electrical energy (induced potential difference). Motor effect: current + field -> force. Generator effect: movement + field -> potential difference/current.
Higher tier link: the same Fleming left-hand rule is used again when you explain how a motor coil rotates.
core.h: Applications and links to other topics
core.p: The motor effect is used wherever electrical energy must be turned into movement. The **electric motor** places a current-carrying coil in a magnetic field, and the forces on its two sides, which act in opposite directions, make the coil spin. A **loudspeaker** places a coil attached to a paper cone in the field of a permanent magnet; the alternating current in the coil changes direction rapidly, so the coil and cone move backwards and forwards and make sound waves. These are covered in the next spec points.

bullets: 1. Current in the wire creates a circular magnetic field around it.
2. This field interacts with the field of the permanent magnet.
3. The two fields add on one side and cancel on the other.
4. A **force** acts on the wire from the stronger to the weaker field, at right angles to both the field and the current.
5. Direction found by Fleming's left-hand rule: thumb force, first finger field, second finger current.
6. Reversing the current or field reverses the force; reversing both does not.
7. The size increases with stronger field, bigger current, or more length of wire in the field.
core.h: Putting it together: a model explanation
core.p: In a longer question you are rewarded for linking ideas in order: the current produces a magnetic field around the wire, this interacts with the field of the magnet, the fields combine to give a stronger field on one side, and the wire is pushed in a direction at right angles to both. Then you can predict what happens if something changes. Practise writing the sequence in your own words until you can do it without notes.

exam: 'State' or 'name' (1 mark): give the term only, e.g. 'the motor effect'. State the unit of magnetic flux density: tesla (T).
'Describe what happens' (2 marks): give direction and what changes, e.g. 'the wire moves (up) at right angles to the field' plus 'the direction reverses if the current is reversed'.
'Give the direction of the force' (1-2 marks): apply Fleming's left-hand rule; say 'up/down/into the page' AND label which finger is which if drawing.

'Explain why the wire moves' (3-4 marks): current makes a magnetic field around the wire -> interacts with the magnet's field -> a force acts on the wire (a catapult field with a stronger and a weaker side).

A 'how could the force be increased' question wants all three: increase the current, use a stronger magnet (greater magnetic flux density), use a longer length of wire in the field. Do not say 'make it bigger'.
'What happens if both are reversed?' Answer: force is the same direction (unchanged).
Use the command word: 'Explain' needs a reason (because), 'Describe' just needs what happens. Link your sentences with 'so', 'because' and 'therefore'.

In a 6-mark question, structure the answer: fields -> interaction -> force direction -> Fleming's rule -> effect of changes. Use the key words 'magnetic flux density', 'conventional current', 'at right angles'.
On diagrams, do dots and crosses correctly: cross into the page, dot out of the page. Draw force arrows clearly with arrowheads.
Higher tier: you may be asked to label a diagram with F, B and I, or to say which way a coil/wire moves; always check the hand with the actual diagram.
Check units: B in tesla, I in amps, l in metres, F in newtons if a calculation follows.

mistakes.r: Use the LEFT hand: thumb = force, first finger = field, second finger = current.
mistakes.w: Using the right hand for Fleming's rule in the motor effect.

mistakes.r: Use conventional current, from positive to negative.
mistakes.w: Using the electron flow direction for the current.

mistakes.r: Field lines go from north to south outside the magnet.
mistakes.w: Saying the field goes from south to north outside the magnet.

mistakes.r: The force is at right angles to both the wire (current) and the magnetic field.
mistakes.w: Saying the force is along the wire or along the field.

mistakes.r: Reversing both leaves the force in the same direction; reversing only one reverses it.
mistakes.w: Thinking reversing both the current and the field reverses the force.

mistakes.r: A wire parallel to the field lines experiences no force.
mistakes.w: Saying a wire parallel to the field has a small force.

mistakes.r: The wire need not be magnetic; the force is due to the interaction of the wire's magnetic field (caused by the current) with the magnet's field.
mistakes.w: Saying the wire is attracted to or repelled by the magnet because it is magnetic.

mistakes.r: The magnet and wire exert equal and opposite forces on each other (Newton's third law).
mistakes.w: Forgetting the magnet also feels a force.

mistakes.r: Motor effect: current in a field gives a force. Generator effect: moving a conductor in a field induces a potential difference.
mistakes.w: Mixing up the motor effect with the generator effect.

summary: You need to know that a current-carrying conductor in a magnetic field feels a force (the motor effect) because the wire's field interacts with the magnet's field, and (Higher tier) use Fleming's left-hand rule to find its direction. It matters because this force drives every electric motor and loudspeaker and is a regular 3 to 6 mark topic.

terms.d: When a conductor carrying a current is placed in a magnetic field, the magnet producing the field and the conductor exert a force on one another.
The region around a magnet or current-carrying wire where a magnetic material or another magnet experiences a force.
Lines showing the direction a free north pole would move; they run from north to south outside a magnet and are closest together where the field is strongest.
A field with parallel, equally spaced field lines, so the same strength and direction at every point (e.g. between flat opposite poles).
A measure of the strength of a magnetic field, measured in tesla (T).
The unit of magnetic flux density.
The direction of current from the positive terminal to the negative terminal of a cell, used when applying Fleming's left-hand rule.
Thumb, first finger and second finger of the left hand held at right angles: thumb = force (motion), first finger = field, second finger = current.
The distorted field produced when the uniform field and the field of the wire combine, strong on one side and weak on the other, pushing the wire towards the weaker side.
Thumb along the conventional current, curled fingers give the direction of the magnetic field around the wire.
When two objects interact, they exert equal and opposite forces on each other.
A force that acts between objects without them touching, such as the magnetic force on the wire.
The induction of a potential difference (and current if the circuit is complete) when a conductor moves relative to a magnetic field, or the field changes; the reverse of the motor effect.
A material, such as a metal wire, that allows an electric current to flow through it.
At right angles (90 degrees) to something; the force is greatest when the wire is perpendicular to the field.

worked.ans: The force acts at right angles to both the field and the current, i.e. into the page (away from the viewer), found with Fleming's left-hand rule: thumb = force, first finger = field (down), second finger = current (to the right).
worked.q: A horizontal wire carries a current from left to right (conventional current) between a north pole above and a south pole below. Use Fleming's left-hand rule to state the direction of the force. [3 marks]
steps: Field direction is from north to south: north is above, south below, so the field points DOWN (first finger down).
Current direction is left to right (second finger pointing right).
Hold the left hand with the first finger down and the second finger right, both at right angles; the thumb then points into the page (away from the viewer).
Check using the axes: F is perpendicular to both B and I, so it must be into or out of the page, not up, down, left or right.

worked.ans: Downwards: (1) reverse the current (swap supply connections); (2) reverse the magnetic field (swap the poles of the magnet). Still upwards: reverse both the current and the magnetic field.
worked.q: A student places a wire between the poles of a magnet and sees it move upwards when the current is switched on. Describe two changes that would make it move downwards and one that would leave it moving upwards. [3 marks]
steps: Reversing the current alone reverses the force: swap the connections on the power supply.
Reversing the field alone reverses the force: turn the magnet round so the poles swap.
Reversing both leaves the force unchanged.

worked.ans: The current in the wire creates a circular magnetic field around it. This interacts with the magnet's field. The fields add together on one side of the wire (stronger field) and cancel on the other side (weaker field), so there is a resultant force on the wire, pushing it towards the weaker field, at right angles to both the wire and the field. (The magnet also experiences an equal and opposite force.)
worked.q: Explain why a current-carrying wire placed at right angles to a uniform magnetic field experiences a force. [4 marks]
steps: The current produces its own magnetic field in circles around the wire.
This field interacts with the uniform field of the magnet.
On one side the fields point the same way and add (stronger); on the other they oppose and cancel (weaker).
The wire is pushed from the stronger to the weaker field region, at right angles to both.
